title: the oldest hello
hook: you've said it after yoga class; the words inside say more than hello
carry: the light in me sees the light in you

segments.voice: Two palms pressed together. It's on your phone's keyboard, between the thumbs-up and the clapping hands. It's how a yoga class ends. It's how a shopkeeper in Chennai greets a customer at the counter, and how a host in New Jersey welcomes a guest through the door. And there's a word that goes with it, a word plenty of people say without a second thought. Namaste. It sounds like a polite hello, and it is one. But it's built out of two older words, and once you hear them, the greeting gets bigger. Today, in a few minutes, you find out what you've been saying.

Break the word open. It's Sanskrit, and the dictionary splits it in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Namaste. I bow to you. That's it. That's the whole literal meaning. So the next question is the interesting one. Bow to what, exactly? Not to your clothes, your job title, or how your day is going. The old texts of this tradition keep pointing inward. One of them, the Chandogya Upanishad, talks about a light that shines above the heavens, higher than everything, in the highest world. And then, in the same breath, it says that this light is the very same light that is inside a person. Out there and in here: one light. Put that next to the greeting, and you get today's line. The light in me sees the light in you. That isn't a dictionary translation of namaste. It's a reading of it, and texts like this one are why the reading makes sense. Notice what that reading assumes about a person. It doesn't open by saying: become worthy first, fix yourself, then come back. Its opening move is that the light is already in there. On a bad day, on no sleep, halfway through a long scroll late at night. Already there. In this reading, the work isn't earning it. It's learning to notice it, in yourself and in whoever is standing across from you. Read that way, a plain hello carries all of it.
screen: `NAMAS — A BOW.` · `TE — TO YOU.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, INSIDE A PERSON.` · `ALREADY IN THERE.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT IN ME SEES THE LIGHT IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. If you'd like, press your palms together in front of your chest. Breathe in, slowly, all the way. And as you breathe out, let your head tip forward, just a little. A small bow. Say the word inside, if you want: namaste. Not to anyone in particular yet. Just to the fact that someone is in here, breathing, and showed up today.
Namaste. I bow to you. And underneath it: the light in me sees the light in you. A word that was already in the air. Now you know what's inside it. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: the light in me sees the light in you. Try it once today, on a friend, a stranger, or the person who's hard to like. You don't have to say it out loud. Just see somebody that way for a second. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods.

fork.setup: the Chandogya Upanishad describes a light shining above the heavens, higher than everything. where does it say that same light is found?
fork.reveal: it says the light above the heavens is the very same light that is within a person. that's the idea behind today's line.

original.note: Sanskrit: namas, a bow, plus te, to you. I bow to you.

trapdoor: what you thought: a yoga-class goodbye.
what it means: I bow to you, and the light in me sees the light in you.
what a scholar hears: namas (a bow) plus te (to you); the light reading leans on texts like Chandogya Upanishad 3.13.7, where the light beyond heaven is the light within a person.

notes: Chandogya Upanishad 3.13.7 (the light that shines above heaven is the same as the light within a person) is paraphrased; confirm the verse number and that the paraphrase is fair.

The script says plainly that 'the light in me sees the light in you' is a reading of namaste, not its literal meaning (namas + te, I bow to you). Keeper may want to name the reading's lineage (e.g. Vedanta) or leave it as is.
